newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. move on phone costs could face WTO fight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. move on phone costs could face WTO fight.

text.p: A United States effort to force other countries to slash the rates they charge for incoming international calls could be challenged in the World Trade Organisation (WTO), trade analysts said on Tuesday.

But developing states, who will be especially hit by the U.S. action, may be reluctant to be seen to fight a measure with built-in provisions to ease the pain of its introduction for them, according to the analysts.

One U.S. move, signalled well before a WTO pact aimed at opening up global telecommunications markets was agreed in Geneva in February, was formalised last Thursday by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in Washington.

The FCC, the country's top phone regulator, decreed that varying ceilings would be set for the amount U.S. phone companies can pay foreign carriers for connecting calls originating in the United States.

The ceilings, or benchmarks, which range from 15 to 23 cents a minute, are at least five or six and up to 10 times below the current levels national, often state monopoly, companies charge for the local link-up.

FCC officials said the measure, once in full effect after the year 2003, would have cut the average price of an international call from the United States to 20 U.S. cents a minute from its current 88 cents.

Taking effect at the start of next year when the WTO pact also goes into operation, it will save U.S. consumers and businesses $17 billion over the next five years alone, and help bring down costs for consumers around the globe, the FCC argues.

It would destroy the long-standing international accounting rates system administered by the also Geneva-based International Telecommunications Union (ITU), which itself recognises new technologies like the Internet make change inevitable.

The benchmarks will be set according to each country's income level and for the poorest -- many of whom rely on income for telephone calls to fund their own local system or other projects -- will be phased in over the next five years.

The some 70 countries who signed up to the WTO deal effectively accepted that Washington would force their hand as the price for getting the United States, the world's biggest telecom market, into the pact.

But some say draft U.S. rules for the implementation of the deal could put Washington in violation of its commitment to most-favoured-nation (MFN) or non-discriminatory treatment of all foreign firms entering the U.S. telecom market.

These rules, yet to be finalised, give backup to the benchmark system by providing for withdrawal of licences from U.S.-established affiliates of foreign companies if their national governments do not meet the benchmarks.

The rules also allow for the FCC to withdraw authorisation from U.S. companies to lease spare capacity on their own circuits to carriers in countries which do not bring their rates down to the levels sought by the United States.
The European Union has already complained, saying the grounds for refusal of licences are only vaguely defined and could be used to discriminate against some foreign companies in favour of others.

But trade analysts say if the United States withdrew licences or authorisation only after they were granted on the grounds that the foreign carriers were using MFN to get round U.S. accounting rates while U.S. firms are kept out of their own market, Washington could be on fairly firm ground.

U.S. officials say they are confident they can defend the rules and the benchmark system if they are brought to the WTO's dispute settlement system -- where decisions by neutral panels and appeals boards are binding.
